doc.title: Sherrie Maricle interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 18, 2001 [interview 1 of 2]

chapter: Jazz education and New York jam sessions
title: New York club scene: the Village Gate and fewer places to play
summary: She played eight years at the Village Gate; clubs and jam sessions have closed, leaving students with nowhere to play.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: I know. Or any musician. So then in the role of teacher sometimes I see really such unbelievable talent in the students. And even in the time I’ve lived in New York and just see the change in the face of jazz there with the shut down of clubs. I played for eight years at the Village Gate, which was a great club on Bleecker Street. Every single Saturday. I mean I got this job like the second year I lived in New York and I had it for eight years, just playing with my own trio. And it was a jam session, it was four hours, it was like unbelievable training for me, speaking to an audience and just, you know, playing all the time. And then that club closed and they used to have jam sessions, the Blue Note had a jam session every night except Monday. Every night ‘til 4 A.M. because I used to go when I first moved, and there were all these loads of opportunities to play. The Village Vanguard was $5 and you could see Mel Lewis’ band. Now the cost is astronomical to go anywhere. The students are struggling, there is nowhere for them to play. Like there’s no outlets for them.

Well that was something I was going to ask you about, especially being one of the things you do with IAJE. I attended the festival in January and it was breathtaking almost to see the amount of people and everybody there. But I wondered, is it translating down to that level of places to play and jam sessions and all that kind of thing?
